what: Protection equivalence: minified+bundled JS via npm (with source maps rigorously excluded per memory 142) provides ~90% of Bun compile's source protection at ~10% of the operational cost. Both expose the same bundled+minified+transpiled JS to a determined attacker — Bun just wraps it in a Mach-O/ELF/PE binary. Delta is ~15-30 min of friction (run `bun-decompile` or `unbuned`) vs instant `cat` on the minified npm file. Content an attacker ends up with is IDENTICAL (minifier output, mangled names, no comments, runnable). Implication for aide-memory binary migration: the ~2-week binary pipeline + ongoing operational burden (5-platform builds, code signing, notarization, AV false-positive handling, corporate-proxy support) is only justified by the NON-PROTECTION benefits — (a) zero-Node-required for users, (b) native-dep embedding beyond better-sqlite3, (c) "real app" UX feel. User stated Node requirement doesn't matter and aide-memory has no native deps beyond better-sqlite3 (which has a bun:sqlite shim anyway). So the binary migration's actual payoff vs minified-npm is: ~20 minutes of additional reverse-engineering friction + marketing feel. Worth reconsidering whether the full binary plan is right, or if minified npm (with javascript-obfuscator layer for extra friction) ships the goal at 1-day cost instead of 2 weeks + ongoing burden.
why: User asked directly "what's the level of security for code on this vs npm finding a way to hide source maps" — research reveals the protection delta is tiny. This fundamentally reframes the binary migration cost-benefit: if source protection is THE goal (per memory 136) and Node-requirement doesn't matter to the user, then 2 weeks + ongoing ops burden may be overkill vs 1 day for minified-npm. Future binary-migration reviewers should weigh this before committing to the full binary plan.
